lessonTitle: Asthma: Variable Obstruction, Stepwise Therapy and Acute Severity

blocks.text: A 17-year-old goalkeeper wakes at 3 a.m. most nights in winter with a dry cough, and wheezes on cold training evenings, yet by morning he feels perfectly fine and his resting spirometry is normal. The symptoms come and go, and that variability is the signature of asthma. This unit shows how to prove variability, treat it in steps, and recognise the night it becomes life-threatening.

blocks.markdown: **Mechanism.** Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways, usually eosinophilic and atopic, with three linked processes: **airway inflammation** (mucosal oedema, mucus), **bronchial hyperresponsiveness** (smooth muscle contracts excessively to triggers such as allergen, cold air, exercise, viral infection) and **reversible airflow obstruction**. Narrowing raises airway resistance (resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of the radius, so small changes in calibre matter), producing wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough that characteristically worsen at night and early morning.

blocks.title: Variable airflow obstruction
blocks.text: Airflow obstruction is shown by a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (below 0.70, or below the lower limit of normal) where FEV1 is the forced expiratory volume in 1 second and FVC the forced vital capacity. Variability is demonstrated by a significant improvement after a bronchodilator (reversibility), by a diurnal variation in peak expiratory flow (PEF) of more than 20% over two weeks of monitoring, or by a response to a trial of treatment. A normal spirometry between attacks does not exclude asthma.

blocks.caption: Objective tests that support asthma. Thresholds follow common UK practice and vary by guideline and laboratory.
rows: FEV1 and FVC before and after salbutamol
FEV1/FVC below 0.70 with FEV1 increase of at least 12% and at least 200 mL
Raised (for example 40 parts per billion or above in adults)

blocks.title: Calculating bronchodilator reversibility
blocks.prompt: A 24-year-old woman with intermittent wheeze has pre-bronchodilator FEV1 2.30 L. After inhaled salbutamol her FEV1 is 2.70 L. Is the response significant?

steps.text: Absolute change: 2.70 - 2.30 = 0.40 L (400 mL), which is above the 200 mL threshold.
Percentage change relative to the starting value: (0.40 / 2.30) x 100 = 17.4%.
Both criteria are met (at least 12% and at least 200 mL), so the obstruction is significantly reversible, supporting asthma.

blocks.answer: Reversibility of 17.4% (400 mL): significant, supporting a diagnosis of asthma.

blocks.markdown:
**Stepwise treatment (o2).** The aims are to control symptoms, prevent exacerbations and avoid dependence on reliever drugs. The principles are:

1. **Reliever** (short-acting beta-2 agonist such as salbutamol, or low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus the fast-acting long-acting beta-agonist formoterol): relaxes bronchial smooth muscle quickly.
2. **Preventer**: an **inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)** reduces inflammation and is the cornerstone. A long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) is never used alone in asthma, because it relieves bronchoconstriction without treating inflammation and has been linked to asthma deaths; it is always combined with an ICS.
3. **Escalation**: if symptoms persist despite good adherence and technique, step up by adding a LABA in a combination inhaler, then a leukotriene receptor antagonist or other options, with specialist referral for difficult asthma. Current UK joint guidance favours an ICS-formoterol combination used both for maintenance and as the reliever (MART), but local formularies and older stepwise schemes differ.
4. **Step down** when control is sustained for three months.

blocks.caption: Inhaler devices and technique points.
rows: Slow deep breath in, hold the breath for about 10 seconds; use a spacer
Pressing and breathing out of phase
Rapid, forceful, deep breath through the device
Slow inhalation, so the powder is not delivered
One puff at a time, breathe in slowly after each
Omitting this risks oral candidiasis and hoarseness

items: Always check adherence, inhaler technique, trigger exposure (including smoking) and comorbid rhinitis before escalating therapy.
Give a personalised written asthma action plan, with PEF or symptom triggers for self-escalation.
Use of a reliever more than about three times a week, or night waking, suggests poor control.
Annual review includes technique, adherence, smoking status and vaccination.

blocks.markdown: **Grading an acute attack (o3).** British Thoracic Society grading uses PEF (as a percentage of the patient's best or predicted value), respiratory rate, pulse, speech and oxygen saturation. **Moderate**: PEF 50 to 75% of best. **Acute severe**: PEF 33 to 50%, respiratory rate 25/min or above, heart rate 110/min or above, or inability to complete sentences in one breath. **Life-threatening**: PEF below 33%, SpO2 below 92%, silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, arrhythmia, exhaustion, altered consciousness, hypotension, or an arterial PaCO2 in the normal range (a normal PaCO2 in an acutely breathless asthmatic signals tiring). **Near-fatal**: raised PaCO2 and/or need for ventilation.

blocks.title: Grading severity from peak flow
blocks.prompt: A 31-year-old man known to have a best PEF of 600 L/min arrives wheezing with PEF 270 L/min, respiratory rate 28/min, pulse 118/min, and can speak only in short phrases. His SpO2 is 95% on air. How severe is the attack?

steps.text: 45% lies in the 33 to 50% band; respiratory rate 28 and pulse 118 also meet the acute-severe criteria.
No life-threatening features are listed (SpO2 above 92%, no silent chest or exhaustion), so the grade is acute severe.

blocks.answer: Acute severe asthma (PEF 45% of best), needing urgent treatment.

items: Nebulised salbutamol (for example 5 mg, a teaching example), repeated as needed; add nebulised ipratropium for severe attacks.
Systemic corticosteroid early (for example oral prednisolone 40 to 50 mg daily in adults for about 5 days, a teaching example, or intravenous hydrocortisone if unable to swallow).
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for severe or life-threatening attacks not responding, with specialist or critical-care involvement.
Reassess with PEF, SpO2 and, in severe cases, arterial blood gases; escalate to intensive care for exhaustion, rising PaCO2 or poor response.

blocks.title: A silent chest and a normal PaCO2 are danger signs
blocks.text: In acute asthma, widespread wheeze means air is still moving. A silent chest means too little air is moving to wheeze. A normal PaCO2 in a breathless patient means the patient is tiring. Treat both as life-threatening.

points: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with hyperresponsiveness and variable obstruction; prove variability with reversibility, serial PEF or FeNO.
ICS is the cornerstone preventer; LABA is never used alone; check adherence and technique before stepping up.
Acute attacks are graded by PEF percentage of best, vital signs, speech and saturation, with silent chest and normal PaCO2 marking life-threatening disease.
Emergency treatment: oxygen to 94-98%, nebulised bronchodilators, early systemic corticosteroid, IV magnesium and critical-care escalation if needed.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has nocturnal cough and wheeze, and a two-week twice-daily peak flow diary shows morning readings repeatedly 25% lower than evening readings. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Diurnal PEF variability above 20% supports a diagnosis of asthma
Variability excludes asthma
A normal chest X-ray rules out asthma
The pattern is typical of fixed airflow limitation

questions.correctOptionText: Diurnal PEF variability above 20% supports a diagnosis of asthma

distractorRationale.a: Correct: marked diurnal variability reflects variable airway narrowing.
distractorRationale.b: Variability is the hallmark of asthma, not an exclusion.
distractorRationale.c: Chest X-ray is usually normal in asthma and does not exclude it.
distractorRationale.d: Fixed obstruction (as in COPD) shows little variability.

questions.explanation: Variable airflow obstruction is the defining physiological feature of asthma, and a diurnal PEF variability above 20% over two weeks demonstrates it. Fixed obstruction would show little change between readings.

questions.stem: A patient is prescribed a dry-powder inhaler. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Breathe in slowly and gently
Breathe in rapidly and deeply through the device
Always use a spacer
Shake the inhaler before every dose

questions.correctOptionText: Breathe in rapidly and deeply through the device

distractorRationale.a: A slow breath is for a pressurised MDI; a dry-powder device needs a fast breath to disperse the powder.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the patient's own inspiratory effort disperses the powder.
distractorRationale.c: Spacers are used with pressurised MDIs, not dry-powder inhalers.
distractorRationale.d: Shaking applies to pressurised MDI canisters.

questions.explanation: Dry-powder inhalers are breath-actuated and rely on a fast, deep inspiration to deaggregate and deliver the drug into the airways. A slow breath, appropriate for a pressurised MDI, delivers little powder.

questions.stem: Why is a long-acting beta-2 agonist not given alone as asthma maintenance therapy?

options.text: It does not relax bronchial smooth muscle
It treats bronchoconstriction but not inflammation, and monotherapy is associated with increased risk of asthma-related death
It causes oral candidiasis
It is only effective in COPD

questions.correctOptionText: It treats bronchoconstriction but not inflammation, and monotherapy is associated with increased risk of asthma-related death

distractorRationale.a: LABAs do relax bronchial smooth muscle; that is their action.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: masking symptoms without suppressing inflammation allows disease to progress unrecognised.
distractorRationale.c: Candidiasis is a local side effect of inhaled corticosteroids.
distractorRationale.d: LABAs are used in both asthma (with ICS) and COPD.

questions.explanation: Asthma is an inflammatory disease, so a bronchodilator alone relieves symptoms while leaving inflammation untreated. For this reason a LABA is combined with an ICS, and monotherapy has been linked to asthma-related deaths.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old on a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid still uses her reliever four times a week and wakes twice weekly with symptoms. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the inhaled corticosteroid
Check adherence and inhaler technique, then step up, for example by adding a long-acting bronchodilator in a combination inhaler with the ICS
Switch to a long-acting beta-agonist alone
Start regular oral prednisolone

questions.correctOptionText: Check adherence and inhaler technique, then step up, for example by adding a long-acting bronchodilator in a combination inhaler with the ICS

distractorRationale.a: Stopping the preventer would worsen control.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: poor control should first prompt a check of adherence and technique before escalation.
distractorRationale.c: LABA monotherapy is avoided in asthma.
distractorRationale.d: Long-term oral steroids are a late option with significant adverse effects.

questions.explanation: Symptoms above target indicate poor control. The stepwise approach checks the common reasons (adherence, technique, triggers) before escalating, and escalation keeps the ICS and adds a LABA only as a combination product.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old known asthmatic is brought in exhausted and barely speaking. PEF is 28% of best, SpO2 is 90% on air and the chest is quiet on auscultation. Arterial PaCO2 is 5.2 kPa (reference about 4.7 to 6.0 kPa). How is this attack graded?

options.text: Moderate
Acute severe
Life-threatening
Controlled, with only mild exacerbation

distractorRationale.a: Moderate has PEF 50 to 75% of best, with no life-threatening signs.
distractorRationale.b: Acute severe has PEF 33 to 50%; here the PEF is below 33% and other features are present.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: PEF below 33%, SpO2 below 92%, silent chest, exhaustion and a normal PaCO2 are life-threatening features.
distractorRationale.d: The patient is clearly unwell and not controlled.

questions.explanation: Any single life-threatening feature classifies the attack as life-threatening, and this patient has several. A normal PaCO2 in a breathless patient is ominous because a patient with severe obstruction should be hyperventilating and hypocapnic, so normocapnia signals fatigue.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has pre-bronchodilator FEV1 of 2.10 L. After salbutamol his FEV1 is 2.55 L. Calculate the percentage improvement in FEV1 relative to the baseline value.
questions.explanation: The change is 2.55 - 2.10 = 0.45 L. Relative to the baseline, 0.45 / 2.10 x 100 = 21.4%. This exceeds the 12% and 200 mL thresholds, so the obstruction is significantly reversible, supporting asthma.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old whose best PEF is 560 L/min presents with an exacerbation and a PEF of 224 L/min. Express her current PEF as a percentage of her best value.
questions.explanation: PEF as a percentage of best = 224 / 560 x 100 = 40%. This lies in the 33 to 50% band, which defines an acute severe attack unless life-threatening features are present.

questions.stem: Describe how you would demonstrate variable airflow obstruction in an adult with a two-month history of nocturnal cough and wheeze. Include the history, the tests and how each result supports asthma.
markingGuide: History: recurrent wheeze, cough, breathlessness, chest tightness; nocturnal or early morning worsening; triggers (allergen, exercise, cold, viral); atopy or family history
Spirometry showing obstructive pattern (FEV1/FVC below 0.70) with reversibility of at least 12% and 200 mL
Serial PEF for two weeks with diurnal variability above 20%
FeNO as a marker of eosinophilic inflammation
Normal spirometry between attacks does not exclude asthma; response to a trial of treatment is supportive
questions.explanation: Asthma is diagnosed by combining a typical history with objective evidence of variability or inflammation, because no single test is perfect. Because symptoms are intermittent, spirometry can be normal when the patient is well and variability has to be sought over time.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with acute severe asthma: PEF 40% of best, respiratory rate 30/min, pulse 120/min. Outline the emergency treatment and the features that would prompt escalation to intensive care.
markingGuide: Early systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone or IV hydrocortisone)
IV magnesium sulfate if severe not responding
Monitor PEF, SpO2, vital signs and arterial blood gases
Escalate to critical care for exhaustion, altered consciousness, rising PaCO2, persistent hypoxia, silent chest or poor response
questions.explanation: Treatment combines rapid bronchodilation with anti-inflammatory therapy and correction of hypoxia. Rising PaCO2 or exhaustion indicates impending respiratory failure and needs senior and intensive care input for possible ventilation.

questions.stem: Explain the stepwise preventer and reliever approach to asthma and give three points of correct inhaler technique or follow-up that improve control.
markingGuide: Reliever (SABA, or fast-acting formoterol with ICS) for symptoms
Inhaled corticosteroid as the cornerstone preventer
Step up by adding a LABA in a combination inhaler, then other agents such as a leukotriene receptor antagonist, with specialist referral
Check adherence, technique and triggers before stepping up; step down when control is sustained
Technique points: spacer with pMDI, fast deep breath with DPI, rinse mouth after ICS, written action plan, annual review
questions.explanation: Stepwise therapy matches intensity to control, with an ICS to treat the underlying inflammation. Many apparent treatment failures reflect poor adherence or technique, so these are reviewed before any escalation.
